parts.text:
draft.tex in the workspace is a short paper draft. Review it with one script program that you write yourself (the script tool's description lists what a program can call):
1. Get the draft's sections through the latex script module.
2. Run two review rounds with self(), each returning a structured verdict that names the section it checked and whether its claim is supported. Round 1 checks the first section; choose round 2's section from round 1's verdict.
3. After both rounds, query the executions SQL history (the runs table) to count how many of your child runs ended completed.
Return an object with the section titles, both verdicts, and that count as completedChildren. Then reply with one sentence on what the review found.

A reviewer might say "supported" (it's a definition/assumption). Hmm, verdict names section and whether claim supported. Round 1 checks Setup. Round 2's section chosen from round 1's verdict.

I should have round 1 return the verdict plus maybe a suggested next section. But instruction: "choose round 2's section from round 1's verdict" — so I decide based on the verdict. If round 1 says not supported, go to Main bound. If supported, go to Discussion or Main bound.

Probably not resolvable in SQL.

I could query runs joined to run_tree where ancestor... Actually run_tree(ancestor_id, id, depth) gives every ancestor of every run. My run's id u—child runs have depth 1 relative to me. I can do:

SELECT count(*) FROM runs r JOIN run_tree t ON t.id = r.id WHERE t.depth = 1 AND r.status='ended' AND r.outcome='completed' ... but that counts for any ancestor. Need to restrict ancestor to me.

Maybe self() results give runId; I can query runs by id and check parent. So: get my children ids from self runId values? No — self's runId is the child's own run id. Then I could check each: SELECT outcome FROM runs WHERE id = ?. But requirement says count how many of my child runs ended completed using the runs table. I can count among self runIds, but "my child runs" more precisely parent_id = my run id.

Let me get my run id: maybe there's a "current" run concept in executions path "/executions/current". The executions tool with path '/executions/current' returns execution summary. That gives id? Probably. But in a script I can call tools.executions({path:'/executions/current'}). Then query.

Simpler: query with a subquery for max started_at? Fragile. Let's try: first run self calls, then inspect DB to find my run id by checking the parent of the self child run ids. That's clean: query SELECT id, parent_id, kind, status, outcome FROM runs WHERE id IN (...). Then use parent_id to count all children of that parent ended completed. That's robust.

But careful: nested self calls inside a script — the child runs get parent_id = my run id? Probably yes, they're launched as tool calls by me.

Also, a subtlety: if I run self calls in a script, the script itself may be re-run after interruption; ids may vary. Fine.

Ask for nextSection? Not needed but useful. I'll ask the child for verdict only; I choose round 2 based on supported: if supported, escalate to the section that depends on it (Main bound). I'll implement logic: if round1.supported, round2 = 'Main bound'; else round2 = 'Discussion' (or 'Main bound' anyway...). That's fine but maybe make logic meaningful: choose the section that carries the load of the first verdict. If supported, go to Main bound since it inherits Setup; if not, still Main bound. Hmm.

Better: ask round 1 verdict to include a "nextSection" recommendation, then choose round 2 from it (I validate against known titles). That satisfies "choose round 2's section from round 1's verdict" literally.

The draft content: I'll pass full draft text of all sections in both prompts, plus the specific section to check.

Also verify: does the paper actually have a real issue? The claim sup_K |f| ≤ 1 for arbitrary continuous f on compact K is false in general (any constant function bigger than 1 contradicts, e.g. f ≡ 2). So Main bound is unsupported/false. Discussion's claim "bound is sharp for constant functions" would require f ≡ 1; sharp means cannot be improved — true only if sup can equal 1... actually not sharp in a meaningful sense. Round 2 on Main bound should flag it.
